title: Motion in a Straight Line — Class 12 NIOS Physics
subject: Physics

slides.title: Motion in a Straight Line
bullets: Class 12 — NIOS Physics
Chapter 2
slides.speaker_notes: Welcome students. We start kinematics — the description of motion. Today's chapter sets up the precise vocabulary and three workhorse equations that the next chapters keep using.

slides.title: What you'll be able to do
bullets: Distinguish distance from displacement.
Compute average / instantaneous velocity and acceleration.
Apply the three kinematic equations.
Solve free-fall problems (max height, time of flight, return velocity).
Read motion off x–t and v–t graphs.
slides.speaker_notes: Read each objective. Ask which feels least familiar.

slides.title: Position, distance, displacement
bullets: Position x = signed coordinate from a chosen origin.
Distance: total path length (scalar, ≥ 0).
Displacement: x_final − x_initial (vector in 1D).
Distance ≥ |displacement|; equality only for unidirectional motion.
Both have SI unit metre.
slides.speaker_notes: Use the 50-m east → 30-m west example: distance = 80 m, displacement = 20 m east.

slides.title: Velocity and speed
bullets: Average velocity = Δx / Δt; average speed = total distance / total time.
Instantaneous velocity v(t) = dx/dt.
Geometrically: slope of x–t graph at that instant.
|average velocity| equals average speed only for unidirectional motion.
SI: m/s.
slides.speaker_notes: Sketch a curved x–t graph and draw a tangent at one point to make the slope-of-tangent picture concrete.

slides.title: Acceleration
bullets: Average a = (v − u) / Δt.
Instantaneous a = dv/dt = slope of v–t graph.
Uniform a: constant magnitude AND direction.
Sign of a is independent of sign of v.
SI: m/s².
slides.speaker_notes: Stress the independence: a body moving in +x can be slowing down (v > 0, a < 0).

slides.title: Three kinematic equations (constant a)
bullets: v = u + at
s = ut + (1/2) a t²
v² = u² + 2 a s
Apply ONLY when a is constant.
s here is displacement, not distance.
slides.speaker_notes: Walk slowly; show that the third comes from eliminating t between the first two.

slides.title: Worked: car decelerating
bullets: u = 25 m/s, decelerates uniformly to rest in 10 s.
Stopping distance: s = (u + v)/2 × t = 12.5 × 10 = 125 m.
Check: s = ut + ½at² = 250 − 125 = 125 m ✓.
Either approach gives the same answer.
slides.speaker_notes: Two routes converge — useful as a sanity check on board-exam-style problems.

slides.title: Free fall
bullets: Near Earth: a = g ≈ 9.8 m/s² downward.
Take 'up' as +; then a = −g.
Time to apex t_up = u / g.
Max height h_max = u² / (2 g).
Time of flight back to launch: 2 u / g.
slides.speaker_notes: Symmetry: speeds at launch and return are equal. Apex is the v=0 instant, but a ≠ 0!

slides.title: Worked: vertical throw
bullets: u = 25 m/s, g = 10 m/s².
Time to apex: 25/10 = 2.5 s.
Max height: 625/20 = 31.25 m.
Time of flight: 5 s.
Velocity at t = 1.5 s: 25 − 15 = 10 m/s (still up).
slides.speaker_notes: Reinforce that the body still has a = −g at the apex even though v = 0 there.

slides.title: Reading motion graphs
bullets: x–t graph: slope = velocity. Horizontal = at rest.
v–t graph: slope = acceleration; area under = displacement.
Straight, sloping x–t = uniform velocity.
Straight, sloping v–t = uniform acceleration.
v–t crossing the time axis = direction reversal.
slides.speaker_notes: The two best diagnostic tools in board exams. Make sure students can do the slope-and-area calculations on a printed graph.

slides.title: Worked: v–t graph problem
bullets: v–t: straight from (0,0) to (8, 16), then horizontal to (12, 16).
Acceleration in first 8 s: 16/8 = 2 m/s².
Total displacement: triangle (½·8·16=64) + rectangle (4·16=64) = 128 m.
Acceleration in last 4 s: zero (horizontal segment).
Total time: 12 s, average speed = 128/12 ≈ 10.67 m/s.
slides.speaker_notes: Students often forget to add the rectangle's area. Stress 'area under graph' = displacement.

slides.title: You try (5 minutes)
bullets: 1. A ball is dropped from 80 m. Time to ground (g = 10).
2. A car decelerates from 30 m/s to 10 m/s in 200 m. Find a.
3. v–t straight from (0, 5) to (4, 25). Find acceleration and displacement.
4. State the formula for h_max for a vertical throw.
Compare with your bench partner.
slides.speaker_notes: Walk the room; common slip is forgetting g acts at the apex too.

slides.title: Quick check
bullets: Q1. Distance and displacement equal? When?
Q2. v at apex of vertical throw?
Q3. Acceleration at apex of vertical throw?
Q4. Slope of v–t graph?
Show your answer on fingers.
slides.speaker_notes: Use show-of-fingers. Address the most-disagreed item.

slides.title: Key takeaways
bullets: Distance scalar; displacement vector. Distance ≥ |displacement|.
v = dx/dt = slope of x–t; a = dv/dt = slope of v–t.
Three kinematic equations: v = u + at; s = ut + ½at²; v² = u² + 2as.
Free fall: a = g, h_max = u²/2g, time of flight = 2u/g.
Area under v–t = displacement.
slides.speaker_notes: End with the takeaways. Hand out the worksheet and announce homework.
